newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Naphtha/Mogas - Spreads under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Asia Naphtha/Mogas - Spreads under pressure.

text.p: Asian naphtha prices extended its gains on Friday and remained in backwardation despite market scepticism of its bull run, while gasoline was steady, unaffected by news of South Korean sales to Saudi Arabia.
But firmer naphtha levels and stagnant gasoline prices were putting further pressure on reforming margins, with the spread between the two light distillates much lower than $2.00 per barrel.
Refiners have already cut reforming output as the spread have fallen below the $4-$5 breakeven costs.
On the Singapore fob market, a trader offered the 95-octane at $23.00 per barrel, around the same levels talked on Thursday.
But buyers were absent amid weak regional demand and ample supplies.
Traders said a Dutch trader had won the Saudi Aramco 98-octane reformate tender at $3.46 per barrel over MidEast naphtha quotes, fob Jubail, lifting July 26-29.

News of South Korea's Ssangyong's deal to export 1.8 million barrels of 95-octane from July-January to Saudi Aramco should ease some of the downward pressure on the market but traders said this was no panacea for the oversupplied Asian market.
"At least some cargoes will move out of Asia so there will be less pressure," a petrol trader said. "But I don't think it will have a major impact with the market so depresssed."
Otherwise, most analysts said Asia has a huge deficit in refined product supplies.
South Korea petrol exports were boosted to up to 1.5 million barrels per month in April when Ssangyong started up its 50,000-bpd residue fluid catalytic cracker (RFCC).
After its deal with Aramco, Ssangyong which normally has one to two 300,000-barrel cargoes available for export each month, might disappear from the spot market, a trader said.
"It depends on domestic demand," he said.
South Korea has been absent from the spot market during the summer months and was not expected to re-emerge until September.
Naphtha was firmer with Singapore swaps settling in a 10-cent-per-barrel backwardation with July quoted firmer at $21.25/$21.35, up from $21.10/$21.20.
On Thursday, July was still at par to August.
The backwardation in Japan's open-spec contract also doubled with first-half September talked at $1.00 per tonne higher than the second-half.
The move baffled many traders as a glut of arb cargoes have been depressing the market since late April.
The contango hit a 17-month record in early May when prompt prices were at least $2.50 lower than the next half-month's quotes.
The sudden recovery of the oversupplied market which has been in contango for three months, was due to Thai buying.

In the past week, Thailand's Aromatics (Thailand) Plc has bought at least six 30,000-tonne cargoes of full-range naphtha from the Mediterranean for prompt delivery between July 4 and August 2, traders said.
The company has purchased naphtha as a temporary measure to replace the use of crude condensate at its 650,000 tonne-per-year petrochemical aromatics plant on the eastern seabord.
Some traders said spreads would stay backwardated if Thailand continued purchasing naphtha instead of condensate as its feedstock.
But others were not optimistic the Thai purchases would support backwardation because only three cargoes have been purchased above normal requirements.
"The only bullish factor is Thailand, and there are still spot avails and the arbitrage window is open," a trader said.
Traders said while Middle East producers were offering spot cargoes to Asia for August, Mediterranean arbitrage cargoes could still arrive in Asia at $4 per tonne below Asian prices.

"It is more psychological than fundamental," said a western trader. "Second-half September/second-half October should go back to flat or even a slight contango. I don't think the Thai buying is the main reason... there is something else going on which I am trying to find out myself."
(Prices are in dollars per barrel)
